title: Challenge: Palindrome Pointers

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only palindrome-pointers program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
When it is non-alphanumeric under the stated ASCII normalization. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `Rust`, the worked program returns `false`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `Never odd or even`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Ignore punctuation and case; return whether the text is a palindrome.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Ignore punctuation and case; return whether the text is a palindrome. On input `Never odd or even`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Compare normalized symbols from the outside inward and skip irrelevant input. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. Two positions move according to a monotone fact: after one comparison, some candidates can be ruled out permanently. Name that fact. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n) time · O(1) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Test pointers meeting, crossing, duplicate values, and the smallest valid input; many off-by-one errors hide there. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `true`. When it is non-alphanumeric under the stated ASCII normalization. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: In Never odd or even, spaces are skipped and matching letters are compared without ASCII case. Each retained pair agrees. A mismatch in abca is decisive; skipping the mismatched letter itself would incorrectly change the task.
